difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the stimulus treats a sufficient condition as though it were necessary and then generalizes from one instance to a population. Two choices match one half of the flaw but not both; the correct answer replicates both moves in a different domain.
stimulus: Nutritionist: Anyone who eats a serving of oily fish each day will lower their risk of heart disease. Mira eats oily fish every day, and her cardiologist tells her that her risk of heart disease is low. It follows that lowering one's risk of heart disease requires daily consumption of oily fish, and that patients who do not eat oily fish must therefore be at elevated risk.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studying two hours a night is enough to pass the bar exam. Daniel studies two hours a night and passed the bar. So studying two hours a night is the only way to pass the bar, and anyone who studies less than that must fail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily meditation reduces stress in those who practice it. Since Hugo reports reduced stress, he probably meditates daily.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regular exercise lowers blood pressure. Regular exercise also improves sleep. So anyone whose blood pressure is low probably sleeps well.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Everyone who trains at high altitude builds endurance. Anika trained at high altitude, so Anika built endurance. Therefore, high-altitude training is widely available to athletes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reading aloud to children improves their vocabulary. Most parents who read aloud to their children are well educated. So well-educated parents produce children with the best vocabularies.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (i) flips sufficient (oily fish is enough to lower risk) into necessary (required), and (ii) generalizes from one person's case to all patients. (A) flips sufficient (two hours is enough to pass) into necessary (only way) and generalizes from Daniel's case to everyone who studies less.
explanations.B: Parallel topic (health habit) but a different flaw — concluding from an effect back to its cause, not a sufficient/necessary swap.
explanations.C: Different flaw — treating two separate effects of one cause as though they caused each other.
explanations.D: Has the right structural opening but the conclusion drifts to an unrelated claim about availability, so the flaw is in the wrong position rather than parallel.
explanations.E: Correlational overreach about educated parents — a different flaw dressed in similar vocabulary.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw combining a part-to-whole (compositional) error with a category shift from 'some' to 'every.' Three choices are surface-parallel; only one replicates both the composition move and the universalization.
stimulus: Each player on the Riverton chess club has won at least one regional tournament. Therefore, the Riverton chess club as a whole has won every regional tournament, and any team that includes a Riverton member is assured of a regional title.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each musician in the Halden Quartet has performed at Carnegie Hall. So the Halden Quartet has performed at Carnegie Hall as an ensemble, and any group that includes a Halden musician must have performed there too.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the dancers in the Astoria company trained in Paris. So the company's style is probably Parisian, and dancers who leave the company will carry that style with them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Velaris law firm has won every major antitrust case it has argued. So each of its partners has personally won a major antitrust case.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each scientist on the Terra team has published in a leading journal. So at least one Terra paper has appeared in a leading journal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every runner on the Corbel track squad has finished a marathon under three hours. Therefore, the squad's average marathon time is under three hours.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: attributes an individual-member property ('won a tournament') to the collective, then extends it universally to any group containing a member. (A) attributes 'performed at Carnegie Hall' from individuals to the quartet and then to any group containing one — identical compound move.
explanations.B: Starts from 'most,' not 'each,' and the flaw is a stylistic generalization rather than a compositional leap.
explanations.C: Reverses the direction — whole-to-part rather than part-to-whole — so the flaw is in the wrong structural position.
explanations.D: Valid inference — if each scientist has published, then at least one paper has appeared. Not flawed at all.
explanations.E: Valid inference — a universal property of members can legitimately yield a claim about the group's average. Not flawed.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: correlation-to-causation fused with a scope shift from a single country to the global economy. Trap choices replicate one move but not the other.
stimulus: In Norway, as the share of electric vehicles on the road has risen, urban air quality has improved. It follows that electric vehicles cause cleaner air, and that worldwide adoption of electric vehicles is therefore the primary means by which humanity will solve global air pollution.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Japan, as broadband speeds have risen, small-business productivity has risen. So faster broadband causes higher productivity, and expanding broadband globally will be the chief driver of worldwide economic growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In Denmark, cycling rates have increased while obesity rates have fallen. So cycling probably causes weight loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In several European countries, reading scores have risen alongside increased library funding. Therefore, library funding must be the main cause of rising literacy in those particular countries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many nations have reduced smoking rates through taxation. Therefore, taxation of unhealthy products is the most effective public-health tool available to governments everywhere.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In Finland, school meal programs are associated with better student health. So Finland's particular meal program improves health, and its specific curriculum should be exported worldwide.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (i) treats a within-one-country correlation as causation, then (ii) inflates a local effect into the primary global solution. (A) replicates both: a Japan-internal correlation treated as causal, then inflated to the chief driver of worldwide economic growth.
explanations.B: Commits only the causation-from-correlation half; no global scope shift.
explanations.C: Stays within the same set of countries and stops at the causal claim. Only half the flaw.
explanations.D: Starts from a generalization across many nations, so the scope shift isn't there; the flaw is different.
explanations.E: Has a geographic expansion but leaps to a curriculum claim the premise doesn't touch — the flaw is a substitution in the conclusion, not a compound correlation/scope error.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw combines equivocation on 'right' (legal right vs. moral entitlement) with an unwarranted move from 'some' to 'all.' Traps include a valid analog and an equivocation without the quantifier move.
stimulus: Legal scholar: Some citizens have a right to carry firearms, in the sense that the law permits them to do so. But a right, properly understood, is a moral entitlement. Therefore, all citizens have a moral entitlement to carry firearms, and any restriction on that entitlement is unjust.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some workers have a duty to report safety violations, in the sense that company policy requires them to. But a duty, properly understood, is a binding moral obligation. Therefore, every worker has a moral obligation to report safety violations, and any worker who does not report them is acting immorally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most judges have a duty to recuse themselves when they have a personal interest in a case. A duty is a moral obligation. Therefore, judges who fail to recuse themselves in such cases act immorally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some drivers have a license to operate commercial trucks, and a license is a form of permission. So every driver has permission to operate commercial trucks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some doctors are authorized to prescribe controlled substances. Since authorization is a form of trust, these doctors are trusted by the community, and patients should therefore follow any of their recommendations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain parents are permitted by law to homeschool their children. Since a legal permission is a form of choice, every parent has the choice to homeschool, and any parent who does not is failing their children.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: equivocates on 'right' (legal permission → moral entitlement) and expands 'some' to 'all,' concluding any restriction is unjust. (A) equivocates on 'duty' (policy-required → moral obligation) and expands 'some' to 'every,' concluding that non-reporters act immorally — identical compound move.
explanations.B: Starts from 'most' and omits the equivocation — duty is already used morally in both premises. The quantifier shift is also minor.
explanations.C: Has the some-to-every move but no equivocation: 'license' and 'permission' aren't being traded on two distinct senses.
explanations.D: Accurate reasoning is disguised as flawed by the final overreach, but the core move is a chained inference about trust, not a sense-shift on a single term.
explanations.E: Equivocates on 'choice,' but the conclusion is a moral indictment that doesn't parallel 'any restriction is unjust' — the flaw lands in a different structural slot.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: absence of evidence treated as evidence of absence, combined with a shift from 'in our samples' to 'in this region.' Several answer choices nail one half but miss the other.
stimulus: Field biologist: In our three summer surveys of the Dorval wetlands, we never observed the marsh wren. Our surveys covered only the eastern portion of the wetlands. Since we did not detect the marsh wren in those surveys, the species must be absent from the wetlands entirely, and conservation plans for the Dorval marsh wren should therefore be canceled.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the field biologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In three spot checks of the company's eastern warehouse, auditors found no expired inventory. Since the auditors did not find expired inventory during those checks, there must be none anywhere in the company, and the firm's expired-inventory write-off policy should be eliminated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several recent dives of the Pelos reef found no evidence of the striped grouper, though divers covered only a small area. It is therefore possible that the species is rarer than previously thought.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys of a small southern district failed to detect the rust moth. Since the rust moth has never been detected there, it must be rare in that district, though it may thrive elsewhere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Audits of the eastern branch of a bank revealed no fraud. So the eastern branch is free of fraud, and the bank's other branches should adopt its procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Our annual inspections of the northern bridge have never uncovered structural defects. The inspections are thorough and cover the whole bridge. So the northern bridge is probably structurally sound, and scheduled inspections can continue at the current interval.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: absence-in-a-partial-survey is treated as absence everywhere, and a policy (conservation) is canceled on that basis. (A) replicates: absence in partial spot checks is treated as absence company-wide, and the write-off policy is eliminated — same compound flaw, same concluding move.
explanations.B: Not flawed — the conclusion is properly hedged ('possible... rarer than previously thought'). Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed.
explanations.C: Half-flaw only: the conclusion is restricted to the district, not overextended, and the 'rare' claim is measured.
explanations.D: Extends a local absence to a local conclusion, then pivots to a recommendation about other branches. The recommended policy change is in the wrong structural slot — it doesn't parallel canceling plans for the very region surveyed.
explanations.E: Not flawed — premises specify thorough coverage of the whole bridge, so the conclusion is warranted.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: a category error (treating a type-level entity as if it behaved like its instances) combined with a hasty generalization. Traps either commit only the category move or only the generalization.
stimulus: The novel, as a literary form, has evolved for over three centuries and continues to adapt to new readers. Since The Windward Letters is a novel, it too must be evolving and adapting to new readers. And since it has sold well this year, novels in general are clearly thriving as never before.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sonnet, as a poetic form, has developed over five centuries and continues to change. Since 'Summer's Hour' is a sonnet, it too must be changing over time. And since it has recently been widely anthologized, sonnets as a form are flourishing more than ever.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blues, as a musical genre, has influenced many later styles. So any given blues song has influenced many later styles, and the blues is the most influential genre of the last century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The string quartet has been a staple of chamber music since Haydn. Since the Velari Quartet is performing tonight, the genre is alive, and string quartets are the most popular chamber form today.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The essay, as a form, has reinvented itself many times. Since 'On the Terrace' is an essay, it reinvents itself. Therefore, individual essays never stay the same from one reading to the next.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The documentary film has always aimed at truth-telling. Since Rivers at Dusk is a documentary, its makers aim at truth-telling. Documentaries remain one of several important film genres.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ascribes a type-level property ('evolving over centuries') to a single instance, then leaps from one work's sales to the flourishing of the entire form. (A) mirrors both moves exactly: type-level change ascribed to one sonnet, then one anthologization used to conclude the form is flourishing.
explanations.B: Commits only the category error (type-level property to every instance); no sales-style leap to the form's flourishing.
explanations.C: The type-to-instance move is weaker (a performance, not a property-transfer), and the final claim is about popularity without the one-instance springboard. Parallel topic, different flaw.
explanations.D: Category error is present, but the conclusion drifts to an implausible claim about essays changing between readings — the flaw is in the wrong structural slot.
explanations.E: Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed — the 'aim at truth-telling' premise arguably does transfer, and the closing claim is measured rather than an overreach.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: confuses percentage change with absolute change, then generalizes from one company's quarter to the entire industry. Students who catch only the percentage/absolute swap will be tempted by a trap that lacks the industry leap.
stimulus: Analyst: Last quarter, Corten Software's profit margin rose by 20 percent, while its rival Bylor's margin rose by only 5 percent. So Corten made far more profit than Bylor last quarter, and the software industry as a whole must be shifting decisively in Corten's favor.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last season, the Adler Bakery's customer count rose 30 percent, while the Madrona Bakery's count rose only 4 percent. So Adler served far more customers than Madrona last season, and the city's bakery market must be turning decisively toward Adler.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This year, Ganz Motors raised prices by 8 percent while Volera raised them by 3 percent. So Ganz's cars now cost more on average than Volera's, and buyers should therefore prefer Volera.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clinic A's patient load grew by 12 percent while Clinic B's grew by 11 percent. So Clinic A now sees more patients than Clinic B, and the regional market favors Clinic A.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Last year, the Haldane School's test scores rose 15 percent, while Crossfield's rose only 5 percent. So Haldane's teachers are better than Crossfield's.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Profit margins at Orell Industries rose sharply last quarter, so Orell probably made more profit than in any previous quarter, and investors are likely to favor Orell in the year ahead.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: confuses a larger percentage rise with a larger absolute amount, then generalizes from one quarter to an industry trend. (A) replicates both: larger percentage rise conflated with larger absolute customer count, then generalized from one bakery's season to the city market.
explanations.B: Percentage/absolute confusion exists but the conclusion is a recommendation for buyers, not an industry trend — the generalization move is in the wrong slot.
explanations.C: The percentages are too close to drive the stimulus's lopsided inference, and the mismatch between 'grew by X%' and 'sees more patients' is different in kind.
explanations.D: Different second flaw — attributing test-score growth to teacher quality rather than generalizing from one year to an industry.
explanations.E: Commits only the generalization half; no percentage-vs-absolute comparison between rivals.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: an ad hominem-adjacent move (dismissing a speaker's argument because of the speaker's profession) combined with a leap from 'no good reason to accept X' to 'X is false.' Traps include a pure ad hominem and a pure absence-to-denial fallacy.
stimulus: Critic: The economist's forecast that inflation will ease by next spring should be dismissed. She works for a bank that profits when borrowers expect low inflation, so her forecast cannot be trusted. Since we therefore have no good reason to accept her forecast, we can conclude that inflation will not ease by next spring.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lawyer's claim that the new statute is constitutional should be dismissed. He is employed by a firm that benefits when the statute is upheld, so his opinion cannot be trusted. Since we therefore have no good reason to accept his claim, we may conclude that the statute is unconstitutional.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The union leader's assertion that wages have stagnated is self-serving, so her assertion can be ignored. Since we can ignore her assertion, wages have not stagnated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pundit supports the tax increase only because his favored party proposed it. So his support is biased, and we should therefore ignore everything he says on any issue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researcher's study of air pollution was funded by an environmental group. Because of that funding, we have reason to scrutinize the methodology, though we should not dismiss the findings outright.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Since the journalist has never lived in the region she reports on, she cannot understand it, and her accounts of the region's politics must be inaccurate, so the region's politics are not as she describes.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: dismisses a forecast on professional-interest grounds and then moves from 'no good reason to accept it' to 'its contrary is true.' (A) mirrors both: dismissal of the lawyer's claim on firm-interest grounds and a move from 'no reason to accept' to 'the statute is unconstitutional.'
explanations.B: Commits the ad-hominem and absence-to-denial moves but compresses them into one step; the 'self-serving' charge isn't tied to a professional interest in the way the stimulus ties it to the bank.
explanations.C: Ad hominem with a different conclusion structure — 'ignore everything he says' broadens the flaw to all topics rather than concluding the contrary of the specific claim.
explanations.D: Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed — the conclusion is measured ('scrutinize, not dismiss'). Not parallel, because the stimulus is flawed and the correct answer must be flawed.
explanations.E: Different opening — an argument from lack of residence rather than professional interest — and the conclusion is an ad hominem-adjacent but distinct move.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: conflating a statistical average with every individual in a group, then drawing a universal policy conclusion. Traps include an average/individual confusion without the policy leap and a valid analog.
stimulus: City planner: The average commute in our city is 28 minutes. Since the average is 28 minutes, every commuter in the city must spend roughly 28 minutes traveling to work each day. Therefore, any transit project that shortens commutes by even a few minutes will benefit every resident equally, and the city should fund only those projects that reduce the average.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the city planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: School board member: The average class size in our district is 24 students. Since the average is 24, every class in the district must have roughly 24 students. Therefore, any policy that lowers class size by even a few students will benefit every student equally, and we should fund only those policies that reduce the average.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average rainfall in our county last year was 32 inches. Since 32 inches is the average, every part of the county received roughly that amount, and farmers in every part should expect comparable yields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The average wage in the restaurant industry is $15 per hour. Since some workers earn less than the average, policies that raise the minimum wage will help the lowest-paid workers most.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average patient at our clinic waits 20 minutes. Since 20 minutes is the average, some patients wait longer and some shorter; our goal should be to reduce the longest waits rather than the average.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The average house price in the neighborhood has risen by 10 percent, so every house has risen by 10 percent, and each owner's equity has risen accordingly.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: treats the average as a property of each individual and then draws a universal policy conclusion that funding should target the average. (A) replicates: the 24-student average is treated as each class's size, and the policy conclusion restricts funding to policies that reduce the average.
explanations.B: Commits only the average/individual confusion; no policy conclusion that restricts funding.
explanations.C: Not flawed — the reasoning correctly notes variance around an average and draws a measured policy inference.
explanations.D: Not flawed — the reasoning distinguishes average from distribution and chooses a reasonable goal.
explanations.E: Commits only the average/individual confusion about house prices with a further equity claim; the policy-funding slot from the stimulus isn't present.

difficultyReason: Compound flaw: treats a speaker's inability to give reasons for a belief as grounds to reject the belief (epistemic category error), and then generalizes to reject a whole body of knowledge. Traps replicate only one of the two moves.
stimulus: Linguist: Native speakers of a language cannot usually articulate the grammatical rules they follow. Since those speakers cannot state the rules, they must not actually know the rules, and the very idea that native speakers possess tacit grammatical knowledge is therefore a myth.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Skilled bicyclists cannot usually articulate the principles of balance they rely on. Since they cannot state the principles, they must not actually know them, and the very idea that cyclists possess tacit motor knowledge is a myth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young children cannot usually explain why stories move them. So stories do not really move children, and adults who claim otherwise are mistaken.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many jazz musicians can improvise without consciously thinking about music theory. This shows that music theory is irrelevant to improvisation, and formal training in theory is a waste of time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Experienced nurses can often detect subtle changes in a patient's condition without stating how they know. Because they cannot articulate the signs, their judgments are unreliable and should not influence clinical decisions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Competent chess players may not be able to articulate all the heuristics they use, but their results nonetheless show that the heuristics are real, so we should study their games carefully.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: moves from 'cannot articulate the rules' to 'does not know the rules,' then rejects the whole category of tacit knowledge as a myth. (A) replicates both: cyclists who cannot state balance principles are said not to know them, and tacit motor knowledge is rejected as a myth.
explanations.B: Different flaw — concludes children aren't moved, not that the category of being moved is mythical. The second move is missing.
explanations.C: Starts from a premise about independence from theory, not an inability to articulate it. The resulting flaw is a different kind of overreach.
explanations.D: Commits the articulation-to-ignorance move but stops at unreliability; doesn't reject the category of tacit clinical knowledge wholesale.
explanations.E: Not flawed — the reasoning correctly separates inability to articulate from absence of knowledge. Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed.
